input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-630: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments and oral/written summaries of research papers are required. Prerequisites:((CSCI-603 or CSCI-605) &CSCI-661) with grades of B or better or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262)&(CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)).If you have earned credit for CSCI-331 or you are currently enrolled in CSCI-331 you won't be permitted to enroll in CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-630]
An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments and oral/written summaries of research papers are required. Prerequisites:((CSCI-603 or CSCI-605) &CSCI-661) with grades of B or better or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262)&(CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)).If you have earned credit for CSCI-331 or you are currently enrolled in CSCI-331 you won't be permitted to enroll in CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: CSCI-630 introduces the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence systems, covering search, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications in computer,
beats.example: Students will explore how search algorithms navigate decision trees to find optimal solutions in robotics navigation tasks.
beats.title: Introduction to AI Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing the course structure: search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and application domains like computer vision and NLP.

beats.claim: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around four phases: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.
beats.example: In a healthcare AI deployment, the Map phase documents the intended use of a diagnostic tool and identifies affected patient populations.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework Overview
beats.visualDirection: Show a four-step circular diagram labeled Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with each node connected to a brief risk-management action.

beats.claim: The Govern phase establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk.
beats.example: A university AI ethics board assigns specific roles for reviewing algorithmic bias in automated grading systems.
beats.title: Govern Phase: Policies and Accountability
beats.visualDirection: Create a table mapping governance roles (e.g., AI ethics board, compliance officer, developers) to accountability responsibilities.

beats.claim: The Map phase documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts.
beats.example: A self-driving car manufacturer maps the operational design domain, specifying weather conditions and traffic scenarios where the system will operate.
beats.title: Map Phase: Context and Impacts
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a contextual mapping matrix with columns for context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts.

beats.claim: The Measure phase uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks.
beats.example: Researchers conduct A/B testing and statistical analysis to measure the fairness and accuracy of a facial recognition model across different demographics.
beats.title: Measure Phase: Risk Analysis Methods
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen graphic: left side shows qualitative risk assessment (e.g., stakeholder interviews), right side shows quantitative metrics (e.g., accuracy, bias scores).

beats.claim: The Manage phase prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring.
beats.example: A financial institution prioritizes high-risk algorithmic trading models for continuous monitoring and allocates resources for real-time anomaly detection.
beats.title: Manage Phase: Prioritization and Monitoring
beats.visualDirection: Show a risk prioritization matrix with axes for likelihood and impact, highlighting high-priority risks requiring immediate monitoring.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels.
beats.example: A spam filter uses supervised learning with labeled email data, whereas customer segmentation uses unsupervised clustering to group users by behavior.
beats.title: Machine Learning Workflows: Supervised vs. Unsupervised
beats.visualDirection: Present a side-by-side comparison chart: supervised learning shows labeled examples mapping to outputs, unsupervised learning shows raw data clustering into groups.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, ensuring consistent transformations via pipelines.
beats.example: A medical imaging pipeline standardizes image dimensions and normalizes pixel values using only the training set statistics before validation.
beats.title: Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Draw a pipeline diagram showing data flowing through preprocessing steps fitted on training data, then applied to validation and test sets without re-fitting.

beats.claim: Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits, and evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors.
beats.example: A fraud detection system uses k-fold cross-validation to assess model stability, with precision and recall metrics weighted to penalize false negatives heavily.
beats.title: Cross-Validation and Evaluation Metrics
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a k-fold cross-validation cycle with data splits rotating through training and validation sets, alongside a metrics comparison table.

beats.claim: AI systems require ongoing monitoring because context and system behavior can change, and robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness must be continuously evaluated.
beats.example: A deployment checklist verifies that the AI system maintains fairness thresholds, logs privacy compliance, and updates monitoring alerts when distribution shift is detected.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist for AI Deployment
beats.visualDirection: Provide a printable checklist template with checkboxes for robustness, privacy, security, transparency, fairness, and monitoring status, aligned with NIST and ML workflow standards.
